title: The Law of Moses
lead: The laws and commands given through Moses at Sinai and in the wilderness, from Exodus 20 to Deuteronomy. Judaism lives by it as Torah, explained in the oral tradition; Christians read it as holy and fulfilled in Christ, and debate how it still applies.

sections.b: The Torah holds several law collections: the Ten Words (Exodus 20:2–17; Deuteronomy 5:6–21), the Covenant Code (Exodus 20:22–23:33), the Priestly laws of the tabernacle and sacrifice (Exodus 25–31; Leviticus 1–16), the Holiness Code (Leviticus 17–26), and the laws of Deuteronomy 12–26. Critical scholars see them as written in different periods and later joined; traditional readers see them as given at Sinai and on the plains of Moab. Later books measure kings and people by "the law of Moses" (Joshua 8:31; 2 Kings 23:25; Nehemiah 8:1).
sections.refs: Exodus 20:22–23:33; Leviticus 17–26; Deuteronomy 12–26; Joshua 8:31; 2 Kings 23:25; Nehemiah 8:1

sections.h: Torah in Judaism and the law in the New Testament
sections.b: For Judaism the Torah is a gift and a delight (Psalm 1:2; Psalm 119:97), studied with the oral tradition of the Mishnah and Talmud. The rabbis counted 613 commandments. In the New Testament Jesus says he came to fulfill the law (Matthew 5:17), the council of Acts 15 frees Gentile believers from circumcision and most of the law, and Paul argues that no one is made right with God by works of the law, while calling the law holy (Romans 3:20; Romans 7:12; Galatians 2:16).
sections.refs: Psalm 1:2; Psalm 119:97; Matthew 5:17–20; Acts 15:1–29; Romans 3:20; Romans 7:12; Galatians 2:16
